Reader's Digest. Founded in 1922 by DeWitt Wallace and Lila Acheson Wallace, it revolutionized magazine publishing by condensing articles from other publications and making them accessible to a mass audience. The magazine pioneered the digest concept by reprinting, condensing, and repackaging articles from hundreds of other sources. Circulation climbed to over ten million in the United States alone, and it was distributed in dozens of languages worldwide. The editorial philosophy emphasized uplifting, practical, and inspirational content. It featured how-to articles, human-interest stories, humor, and condensed books. Famous sections included Humor in Uniform, Toward More Picturesque Speech, and Most Unforgettable Character I've Met. Reader's Digest was aggressively marketed to rural and small-town America, becoming synonymous with middle-American values. The magazine published condensed books, abridged versions of bestsellers, which became a major revenue stream and influenced American reading habits. Reader's Digest maintained a conservative, patriotic stance throughout its history, avoiding controversial social and political topics. As a publication, it reached broader demographics than any competing magazine, pioneered the digest format and condensed-book business model, and shaped middle-American taste and values.
